b: For many veterans, coming home from military service is only the beginning of another difficult journey. The transition from the structure, camaraderie, and shared purpose of military life to the challenges of civilian life can be overwhelming. Physical injuries, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), depression, anxiety, and feelings of isolation can make it difficult to find a new sense of direction. While there are many programs designed to help veterans navigate this transition, one unlikely source of healing has made a tremendous difference in the lives of many: fishing.

Few events illustrate fishing’s power to change lives like the annual Manhattan Cup, held in New York Harbor’s surrounding waters. This charitable fishing tournament unites professional fishing captains, boat owners, volunteers, sponsors, and veterans for a day on the water. But the Manhattan Cup is about much more than catching fish or winning trophies. It is about camaraderie, connection, and reminding veterans that they are not alone.

The Manhattan Cup came about in the aftermath of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks as a way to support first responders suffering from PTSD. Over time, its mission expanded to include military veterans, particularly those returning from deployments in Iraq and Afghanistan. Today, the tournament is a powerful example of a community harnessing its passion for fishing to make a meaningful difference.

Each year, dozens of charter captains and private boat owners donate their vessels, time, and expertise to take veterans and participating anglers fishing for striped bass and bluefish. The boats depart near the Statue of Liberty and head into the waters of New York Harbor. Although the tournament features competitive divisions and awards for the largest fish, the real victories happen beyond the weigh-in. For veterans struggling with the transition to civilian life, a day on the water can provide something that is often difficult to find elsewhere: a sense of belonging.

One of the tournament’s most important commitments is its Catch 22 initiative. That effort recognizes the widely cited statistic that an average of 22 veterans die by suicide each day, based on historical estimates. Organizers committed to hosting at least 22 veterans at the tournament. Their goal is to ensure that those veterans would have a day filled with friendship, support, and positive experiences. As tournament organizer Gary Caputi has explained, fishing alongside people who appreciate military service and personal sacrifices can open an entirely new world for veterans, many of whom have never fished before.

Perhaps no story better illustrates the life-changing potential of the Manhattan Cup than that of retired Army Sergeant Robert “Nico” Gil. An improvised explosive device blast severely injured Gil, who served multiple tours in Iraq with the 1st Brigade Combat Team, 1st Armored Division. His military decorations included the Purple Heart, Army Commendation for Valor, and Bronze Star for Valor. In 2015, while recovering at a VA hospital, a superior officer brought him to the Manhattan Cup. Gil had never been fishing before. That day, he not only won the tournament but also discovered something that would change the direction of his life. He has credited the experience with helping turn his life around during one of his darkest periods.

Gil then made it his mission to introduce other veterans to the benefits of fishing and the outdoors. He eventually became the Manhattan Cup’s official warrior liaison. Additionally, he established Fin Chaser Warriors Outdoors, an outreach program that helps veterans discover the opportunities for friendship, healing, and renewed purpose that fishing had provided him. His story demonstrates how one positive experience can create a ripple effect, inspiring veterans to help other veterans and extending the impact of a single fishing trip far beyond the original event.

The benefits of fishing go well beyond the Manhattan Cup. Fishing encourages patience, focus, and the ability to slow down and live in the moment. Some might even call that “mindfulness,” letting people step away from stressors and just focus on the fish. It can provide a much-needed break from the thoughts and challenges that can come with life after military service.

Fishing also brings people together and creates opportunities to talk, build friendships, and connect without having to share personal struggles. Sometimes, you don’t need to say much at all. Just spending time with someone who understands can make a world of difference.

For veterans who have spent years serving alongside others, the loss of military camaraderie can be particularly difficult. The relationships formed during military service are often built on trust, shared experiences, and a common mission. Returning home means leaving much of that behind. Fishing can help fill that void by introducing veterans to a new community sharing their interests and appreciating their experiences. A fishing trip can become the beginning of a friendship, a regular routine, or even a new purpose in life.

The Manhattan Cup shows that helping veterans transition from military service does not always require complicated programs or elaborate solutions. It can begin with an invitation to spend a day on the water, a fishing rod placed in someone’s hands, and a community willing to make room for a new friend. For some veterans, it’s the beginning of a new hobby, a lasting friendship, or a renewed sense of purpose. For others like Gil, that invitation can become a turning point.

The Manhattan Cup is part of a growing movement of organizations that embrace fishing and outdoor recreation to support veterans. Groups such as Heroes on the Water, Project Healing Waters Fly Fishing, Take a Vet Fishing, and NPLB (No Person Left Behind) Outdoors provide opportunities for veterans to participate in kayak fishing, fly fishing, guided excursions, and adaptive fishing programs. These organizations demonstrate that the benefits of fishing are not limited to a single tournament or geographic location. Whether it is a veteran learning to tie a fly, casting from a kayak, fishing aboard a charter boat, or spending a quiet afternoon on a river, the opportunity to reconnect with the outdoors can have a lasting impact.

Each organization offers opportunities for individuals, businesses, fishing clubs, outdoor enthusiasts, and community groups to get involved. Financial contributions are important, of course. But so are donating equipment, volunteering time, providing transportation, organizing fundraisers, and sponsoring fishing trips can be equally valuable.

Heroes on the Water is a nonprofit organization that provides free kayak fishing and outdoor recreational experiences for veterans, active-duty military personnel, first responders, and their families. Through a network of volunteer-led chapters, the organization hosts fishing events that encourage relaxation, friendship, and community involvement. People can support its mission through monetary donations, monthly contributions, volunteering at local events, donating kayaks and fishing equipment, sponsoring fishing outings, or helping establish and support local chapters. Fishing enthusiasts, kayak owners, and outdoor recreation businesses can make particularly meaningful contributions by donating their time, equipment, and expertise.

Take a Vet Fishing provides veterans with free recreational fishing experiences while also supporting other needs. That additional support can include assistance with PTSD treatment. Since its founding in 2011, the organization reports taking thousands of veterans fishing. It’s also connected participants with professional fishing guides, experienced anglers, and volunteers who help make these outings possible. Helpful contributions include monetary donations, volunteering as fishing guides or event assistants, donating boats, vehicles, and fishing equipment, sponsoring fishing trips, and organizing community fundraisers.

NPLB Outdoors focuses on providing outdoor recreational opportunities for wounded, injured, and ill veterans. Its emphasis is on making activities accessible to those with physical disabilities. Its fishing programs include freshwater and saltwater excursions, adaptive fishing equipment, and individualized assistance from experienced guides and volunteers. People can support NPLB Outdoors through financial donations, equipment and supply contributions, volunteering as fishing guides or assistants, providing boats and transportation, sponsoring trips, and organizing fundraising events. Both organizations offer opportunities for fishing enthusiasts, boat owners, businesses, and community groups to directly impact veterans’ lives.

Project Healing Waters Fly Fishing is a nationally recognized nonprofit dedicated to the physical and emotional rehabilitation of disabled active-duty military personnel and veterans through fly fishing. Its programs provide instruction in fly tying, casting, rod building, and other fishing skills. It also provides opportunities to participate in fishing outings and develop lasting friendships. Individuals can contribute through one-time or recurring financial donations, volunteering as fly-fishing instructors or mentors, assisting with fishing trips, and donating rods, reels, fly-tying materials, and other supplies. Fishing clubs, outdoor retailers, and businesses can also support the organization through corporate sponsorships, fundraising events, and equipment donations.

This is by no means a comprehensive list. There are many more orgs that embrace fishing to help veterans transition to civilian life. Look for some in your local area, and get involved. After participating in the Manhattan Cup, I’ve seen just how impactful it can be — for both former service members and volunteers.
